extracted.intended_audience: educated readers interested in philosophy, medicine, and conduct under illness (general readers of Montaigne)
extracted.subtask_description: A reflective personal essay about suffering, physicians, and how one should comport oneself under disease; mixes practical advice, sceptical argument, and anecdote. Useful as guidance on conduct in illness and critique of medical practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophy should govern interior conduct, not external appearance
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophy has respect only to life and effects; it need not trouble itself about external appearances or ceremonial composure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: “What matter the wringing of our hands, if we do not wring our thoughts?... She forms us for ourselves, not for others, to be, not to seem; let her be satisfied with governing our understanding.” Allow gestures, sighs, sobs, turning pale, and other vocal frailties so long as courage remains undaunted and tones are not expressive of despair.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permit natural expression of pain if it relieves the body
rubrics_metrics.description: If complaining, roaring, or loud outcries seem to relieve or divert the torments, let them happen rather than command silence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epicurus not only forgives his sage for crying out in torments but advises him to it. Examples: boxers groan to focus the body; some physicians hold loud outcries help women in delivery. In extreme accidents it is cruelty to require exact composedness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain the capacity for rational thought during suffering
rubrics_metrics.description: Even in the depth of suffering one should preserve the ability to speak, think, and give rational answers; pain may trouble but not wholly incapacitate reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne notes he can set a discourse on foot even when in greatest torment and can do sudden endeavours though not for long; the aim is to keep the soul in a condition to know itself and follow its accustomed way.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use premeditation to lessen the terror of illness
rubrics_metrics.description: Meditation and anticipation of possible sufferings prepare the mind so new forms of suffering do not surprise or unman it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted: “No new shape of suffering can arise new or unexpected; I have anticipated all, and acted them over beforehand in my mind.” This mental preparation helps sustain the soul when bodily alarms arise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer experience and common-sense remedies over elaborate medical inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Respect Nature's simple remedies and be suspicious of the inventions of the mind that abandon natural rules and moderation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne accepts simples that moisten or dry and ordinary diet as 'physic' (e.g., mutton, wine) but mistrusts extravagant pharmaceutical concoctions and artificial innovations that depart from natural practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive or frequent use of physic (especially purging)
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent prescriptions corrupt health; purging is among the worst natural motions to provoke and should be used only in the extremest necessity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘Tis from Plato that of three sorts of motions natural to us, purging is the worst. Montaigne observes that many become more often sick and longer in sickness because they take much physic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let nature run its course; avoid violent oppositions between drug and disease
rubrics_metrics.description: The way of living must gently dissolve the disease; violent contest between drug and disease is often to our loss.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘Tis to much purpose we cry out 'Bihore'—a way to make us hoarse but not to hasten the matter. The general order of things cares for men as it does for fleas and moles; follow it rather than try to corrupt its process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be sceptical of physicians’ self-attributed credit and excuses for failures
rubrics_metrics.description: Physicians tend to attribute good outcomes to their remedies and to excuse failures by blaming trivial patient circumstances; therefore view their claims critically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne recounts physicians blaming a patient's posture or a draft for bad outcomes and usurping credit for recoveries that may have happened without them. He cites Plato: physicians are the only men who might lie at pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patient confidence in the physician matters
rubrics_metrics.description: A physician whom the patient trusts may be more effective in practice than a more learned physician who lacks the patient's confidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The patient’s belief prepossesses them with good hope; Montaigne notes that this rule is held so far that an inexperienced physician trusted by the patient may be preferred to an expert not trusted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid magical, superstitious, or exotic remedies without reason
rubrics_metrics.description: Be suspicious of remedies based on superstition (e.g., tortoise foot, lizard urine) or on rare/exotic provenance rather than sound evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne ridicules prescriptions like the dung of rats, the left foot of a tortoise, or blood drawn under the right wing of a white pigeon; he criticises odd numbers of pills and astrological timings for gathering simples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit the number of consulting physicians to avoid conflicting treatments
rubrics_metrics.description: Only one physician should undertake a sick person; multiple physicians produce contradiction, additions and subtractions to remedies, and increase risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When many physicians consult, they contradict one another and expose the patient to confused or harmful care; one physician's default is less scandalous and one man’s success brings clearer glory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the great theoretical disagreement and uncertainty within medicine
rubrics_metrics.description: Medical schools and authors disagree radically on causes and treatments; medicine is the most uncertain practical science and should be treated with humility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne lists competing theories (humours, blood of arteries, atoms of pores, spirits, etc.) and notes continuous overturning: Hippocrates, Chrysippus, Erasistratus, Empirics, Paracelsus, etc. This history counsels caution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer surgical certainty when a condition is palpable and diagnosable
rubrics_metrics.description: Surgery, which sees and feels what it does, is in some cases more certain than speculative physicians who must infer hidden conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a man cut for the stone who had little stone; another bishop cut who had malady in kidneys—yet Montaigne contends surgery is less conjectural because it perceives directly, unlike physicians who lack a 'speculum matricis'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be wary of complex mixed medicines claiming multiple targeted virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: It is implausible that components in a mixed potion will separate their virtues and travel to perform distinct errands unconfounded; mixtures may corrupt faculties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne argues that a potion claimed to heat the stomach and cool the liver, or to go only to the kidneys, is like a bundle of things whose faculties will 'corrupt, confound, and spoil one another.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not force medicines on those who loathe them; aversion can harm
rubrics_metrics.description: Forcing disliked medicines on someone who loathes their taste is dangerous and prejudicial, as aversion itself disturbs the sick person's repose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne explicitly notes that for those who loathe the taste of physic, forcing it down is a harmful endeavour that marvelously distempers them when they most need repose.
